blog_posts.title: How to hire an architect remotely — and get a permit-ready set
blog_posts.dek: A step-by-step walkthrough of vetting licensure, scoping your project, and paying safely through escrow — without a single in-person meeting.

blog_posts.author: Maya E., AIA

blocks.text: Hiring an architect used to mean a stack of in-person meetings before you even knew a price. It doesn't anymore. Here's how to vet licensure, scope your project, and pay safely — entirely remotely — and still walk away with a stamped, permit-ready set.
1. Confirm the license before anything else

A drawing set is only worth submitting if it's stamped by an architect licensed in the state where you're building. That's not a formality — an unlicensed set will be rejected at plan check, no matter how good the design looks.

Ask for the license number and the issuing state, then verify it against the state board's public registry. On our platform this is done for you: every match is verified as actively licensed in your state before it ever reaches you.
Before pricing means anything, both sides need to agree on what's being drawn. A tight scope prevents the two most common blow-ups: surprise costs and missed drawings at permit time.
A complete residential scope usually covers:

Existing conditions (as-built plans or a recent survey)
Proposed floor plans, elevations, and a site plan
Structural coordination and any required calculations
Energy-code compliance for your jurisdiction
A permit-ready, stamped set as the deliverable
3. Get a real number up front

"It depends" is not a quote. Modern platforms price a drawing set from square footage, add-ons, and a jurisdiction complexity score, giving you an itemized range before you talk to anyone. Use that as your baseline, then let each architect confirm a fixed quote or hourly rate on the scoping call.
See your project's estimate in 2 minutes
4. Pay through escrow, not up front

Remote work only feels safe when the money does too. Escrow holds your funds and releases them as you approve milestones — so you're never paying for work you haven't seen. Avoid any arrangement that asks for the full fee before drawings begin.
The best remote projects feel boring — clear scope, a real number, milestones that release on approval. Boring is what gets you a clean permit.
5. Keep a tracked timeline to permit

Once drawings are underway, everything should live in one place: files, comments, milestone approvals, and the submission itself. A tracked timeline keeps revision cycles short and gives your contractor a set they recognize — which is what clears plan check the first time.
Do these five things and remote hiring isn't a compromise — it's faster, cheaper, and just as accountable as walking into a firm's office.

case_studies.title: A 640 sq ft ADU that cleared plan check first try
case_studies.dek: How an Oakland homeowner turned a steep, seismic hillside lot into permit-ready rental income — matched with a licensed architect and delivered entirely remotely.
case_studies.excerpt: A homeowner wanted a rental-income unit on a steep East Bay lot. We matched them with a CA-licensed architect who handled seismic detailing and Title-24 remotely — stamped, submitted, and approved without a single revision cycle.
case_studies.brief: Turn an unused hillside backyard into a 640 sq ft, one-bedroom accessory dwelling unit for long-term rental income — with a stamped set that would clear Oakland plan check without a costly revision loop.
case_studies.challenge1: The lot sloped steeply and sat inside a designated seismic hazard zone, which meant the ADU needed careful foundation and lateral detailing before the city would even look at it. The homeowner had already been quoted vague, open-ended fees by two local firms and wanted cost certainty before committing.
case_studies.challenge2: They also had no interest in a string of in-person meetings. The whole project needed to run remotely — scoping, drawings, revisions, and submission — without ever slowing down.
case_studies.match_narrative: The estimate engine priced the drawing set from square footage, add-ons, and Oakland's jurisdiction complexity score, returning a fixed-quote range up front. Within 48 hours the homeowner was reviewing two CA-licensed architects with hillside ADU experience.
match_points: Both architects verified as actively licensed in California
Filtered for seismic-zone and hillside foundation experience
Fixed quote confirmed on a 30-minute scoping call
Funds held in escrow, released on milestone approval
case_studies.quote: The estimate matched the final quote almost exactly. Our architect was licensed right here in Oakland, and the permit set cleared first try — no revisions.
case_studies.outcome1: The architect delivered a complete, stamped set — floor plans, elevations, a site plan with the hillside grading, structural coordination, and Title-24 energy compliance — six weeks after the scoping call.
case_studies.outcome2: Oakland approved the submission on the first pass, with no revision cycle. The homeowner broke ground the following month, on budget and on the original timeline.

sections.heading: 1. Information we collect
sections.body:
Account and project information you provide — name, email, project type, location, square footage, scope and timeline — used to generate estimates and match you with architects.

Communications and files exchanged on-platform, including messages, drawings, comments and milestone approvals, so both sides have a single record of the engagement.

Usage and device data collected automatically, such as pages viewed, approximate location, browser and device type, to keep the service secure and improve it.

sections.heading: 2. How we use information
sections.body:
To operate the marketplace: pricing your project, surfacing qualified architects licensed in your jurisdiction, and facilitating scoping, payments and delivery.

To protect the platform through escrow, licensure verification, fraud prevention, and enforcement of our terms.

To communicate with you about your projects, and — where permitted — about relevant guides, features and offers you can opt out of at any time.

sections.heading: 3. How information is shared
sections.body:
With the architects you are matched with, limited to what they need to scope and deliver your project. Personal contact details stay on-platform until you engage.

With service providers that process payments, host data, and support operations under contract, and with authorities where required by law.

We do not sell your personal information.

sections.heading: 4. Jurisdiction data
sections.body: Our jurisdiction database scores cities and counties on permit complexity using public regulatory sources. Your individual project location is used to price and match, and is never published as part of that database.

sections.heading: 5. Your choices & rights
sections.body:
You can access, correct, export or delete your account information, and opt out of marketing communications. Depending on your state, you may have additional rights under laws such as the CCPA/CPRA.

To exercise any of these, contact us at privacy@architecthire.com. We will verify your request and respond within the time required by applicable law.

sections.heading: 6. Data security & retention
sections.body:
We use administrative, technical and physical safeguards appropriate to the sensitivity of the data, including encryption in transit. No system is perfectly secure, but we work to protect your information and limit access to those who need it.

We retain information for as long as your account is active and as needed to provide the service, comply with legal obligations, resolve disputes and enforce agreements.

sections.heading: 7. Changes to this policy
sections.body: We may update this policy from time to time. Material changes will be posted here with an updated date, and where appropriate we will notify you directly.
